{{Short description|Sigma-algebra used in probability and ergodic theory}}

In [[mathematics]], especially in [[probability theory]] and [[ergodic theory]], the '''invariant sigma-algebra''' is a [[sigma-algebra]] formed by sets which are [[invariant set|invariant]] under a [[group action]] or [[dynamical system]]. It can be interpreted as of being "indifferent" to the dynamics.

The invariant sigma-algebra appears in the study of [[ergodic systems]], as well as in theorems of [[probability theory]] such as [[de Finetti's theorem]] and the [[Hewitt-Savage zero-one law|Hewitt-Savage law]].

== Definition ==

=== Strictly invariant sets ===

Let <math>(X,\mathcal{F})</math> be a [[measurable space]], and let <math>T:(X,\mathcal{F})\to(X,\mathcal{F})</math> be a [[measurable function]]. A measurable subset <math>S\in \mathcal{F}</math> is called [[invariant set|'''invariant''']] if and only if <math>T^{-1}(S)=S</math>.<ref name=billingsley>{{harvp|Billingsley|1995|pages=313-314}}</ref><ref name="douc">{{harvp|Douc|Moulines|Priouret|Soulier|2018|page=99}}</ref><ref name="klenke">{{harvp|Klenke|2020|page=494-495}}</ref>
Equivalently, if for every <math>x\in X</math>, we have that <math>x\in S</math> if and only if <math>T(x)\in S</math>.

More generally, let <math>M</math> be a [[group (mathematics)|group]] or a [[monoid]], let <math>\alpha:M\times X\to X</math> be a [[monoid action]], and denote the action of <math>m\in M</math> on <math>X</math> by <math>\alpha_m:X\to X</math>. 
A subset <math>S\subseteq X</math> is '''<math>\alpha</math>-invariant''' if for every <math>m\in M</math>, <math>\alpha_m^{-1}(S) = S</math>.

=== Almost surely invariant sets ===

Let <math>(X,\mathcal{F})</math> be a [[measurable space]], and let <math>T:(X,\mathcal{F})\to(X,\mathcal{F})</math> be a [[measurable function]]. A measurable subset (event) <math>S\in \mathcal{F}</math> is called '''almost surely [[invariant set|invariant]]''' if and only if its [[indicator function]] <math>1_S</math> is [[almost surely]] equal to the indicator function <math>1_{T^{-1}(S)}</math>.<ref name ="viana">{{harvp|Viana|Oliveira|2016|page=94}}</ref><ref name="durrett">{{harvp|Durrett|2010|page=330}}</ref><ref name="klenke"/>

Similarly, given a measure-preserving [[Markov kernel]] <math>k:(X,\mathcal{F},p)\to(X,\mathcal{F},p)</math>, we call an event <math>S\in\mathcal{F}</math> '''almost surely invariant''' if and only if <math>k(S\mid x) = 1_S(x)</math> for almost all <math>x\in X</math>.

As for the case of strictly invariant sets, the definition can be extended to an arbitrary group or monoid action.

In many cases, almost surely invariant sets differ by invariant sets only by a [[null set]] (see  below).

=== Sigma-algebra structure ===

Both strictly invariant sets and almost surely invariant sets are closed under taking countable unions and complements, and hence they form [[sigma-algebra]]s. 
These sigma-algebras are usually called either the '''invariant sigma-algebra''' or the '''sigma-algebra of invariant events''', both in the strict case and in the almost sure case, depending on the author.<ref name=billingsley/><ref name="douc"/><ref name="klenke"/><ref name ="viana"/><ref name="durrett"/>
For the purpose of the article, let's denote by <math>\mathcal{I}</math> the sigma-algebra of strictly invariant sets, and by <math>\tilde{\mathcal{I}}</math> the sigma-algebra of almost surely invariant sets.

== Properties ==

* Given a measure-preserving function <math>T:(X,\mathcal{A},p)\to (X,\mathcal{A},p)</math>, a set <math>A\in\mathcal{A}</math> is almost surely invariant if and only if there exists a strictly invariant set <math>A'\in\mathcal{I}</math> such that <math>p(A\triangle A')=0</math>.<ref>{{harvp|Viana|Oliveira|2016|page=3}}</ref><ref name="durrett"/>

* Given measurable functions <math>T:(X,\mathcal{A})\to (X,\mathcal{A})</math> and <math>f:(X,\mathcal{A})\to(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B})</math>, we have that <math>f</math> is [[invariant (mathematics)|invariant]], meaning that <math>f\circ T=f</math>, if and only if it is <math>\mathcal{I}</math>-measurable.<ref name="douc"/><ref name="klenke"/><ref name="durrett"/> The same is true replacing <math>(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B})</math> with any [[measurable space]] where the [[sigma-algebra]] separates points.

* An [[invariant measure]] <math>p</math> is (by definition) [[Ergodicity#Ergodic measure|ergodic]] if and only if for every invariant subset <math>A\in\mathcal{I}</math>, <math>p(A)=0</math> or <math>p(A)=1</math>.<ref name="billingsley"/><ref name="klenke"/><ref name="durrett"/><ref>{{harvp|Douc|Moulines|Priouret|Soulier|2018|page=102}}</ref><ref>{{harvp|Viana|Oliveira|2016|page=95}}</ref>

== Examples ==

=== Exchangeable sigma-algebra ===

Given a measurable space <math>(X,\mathcal{A})</math>, denote by <math>(X^\mathbb{N},\mathcal{A}^{\otimes\mathbb{N}})</math> be the countable [[cartesian product|cartesian power]] of <math>X</math>, equipped with the [[product sigma-algebra]]. 
We can view <math>X^\mathbb{N}</math> as the space of infinite sequences of elements of <math>X</math>,
:<math>
X^\mathbb{N} = \{(x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots), x_i\in X\}.
</math>
Consider now the group <math>S_\infty</math> of '''finite [[permutations]]''' of <math>\mathbb{N}</math>, i.e. [[bijection]]s <math>\sigma:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}</math> such that <math>\sigma(n)\ne n</math> only for finitely many <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math>.
Each finite permutation <math>\sigma</math> acts measurably on <math>X^\mathbb{N}</math> by permuting the components, and so we have an action of the countable group <math>S_\infty</math> on <math>X^\mathbb{N}</math>.

An invariant event for this sigma-algebra is often called an '''exchangeable event''' or '''symmetric event''', and the sigma-algebra of invariant events is often called the '''exchangeable sigma-algebra'''.
A [[random variable]] on <math>X^\mathbb{N}</math> is exchangeable (i.e. permutation-invariant) if and only if it is measurable for the exchangeable sigma-algebra. 

The exchangeable sigma-algebra plays a role in the [[Hewitt-Savage zero-one law]], which can be equivalently stated by saying that for every [[probability measure]] <math>p</math> on <math>(X,\mathcal{A})</math>, the [[product measure]] <math>p^{\otimes\mathbb{N}}</math> on <math>X^\mathbb{N}</math> assigns to each exchangeable event probability either zero or one.<ref name="hewitt-savage">{{harvp|Hewitt|Savage|1955}}</ref>
Equivalently, for the measure <math>p^{\otimes\mathbb{N}}</math>, every exchangeable random variable on <math>X^\mathbb{N}</math> is almost surely constant.

It also plays a role in the [[de Finetti theorem]].<ref name="hewitt-savage"/>

=== Shift-invariant sigma-algebra ===

As in the example above, given a measurable space <math>(X,\mathcal{A})</math>, consider the countably infinite cartesian product <math>(X^\mathbb{N},\mathcal{A}^{\otimes\mathbb{N}})</math>.
Consider now the [[shift space|shift]] map <math>T:X^\mathbb{N}\to X^\mathbb{N}</math> given by mapping <math>(x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots)\in X^\mathbb{N}</math> to <math>(x_1,x_2,x_3,\dots)\in X^\mathbb{N}</math>. 
An invariant event for this sigma-algebra is called a '''shift-invariant event''', and the resulting sigma-algebra is sometimes called the '''shift-invariant sigma-algebra'''. 

This sigma-algebra is related to the one of [[tail event]]s, which is given by the following intersection,
:<math>
\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \left( \bigotimes_{m\ge n} \mathcal{A}_m \right),
</math>
where <math>\mathcal{A}_m\subseteq \mathcal{A}^{\otimes\mathbb{N}}</math> is the sigma-algebra induced on <math>X^\mathbb{N}</math> by the projection on the <math>m</math>-th component <math>\pi_m:(X^\mathbb{N},\mathcal{A}^{\otimes\mathbb{N}})\to(X,\mathcal{A})</math>.

Every shift-invariant event is a tail event, but the converse is not true.
